packageRules.description: OCI Helm charts: the flux manager resolves them through the docker datasource, so docker:pinDigests (from config:best-practices) asks for a chart digest -- and a HelmRelease's chart.spec.version has nowhere to put one. The write is verified as missing, Renovate logs 'Error updating branch: update failure', and abandons the WHOLE branch. Because every pin update shares the single renovate/pin-dependencies branch, this silently held every image digest pin in the repo hostage for as long as an OCI chart was in it. Found with a debug dry run on 2026-09-18.

The kubectl tag in the controller's ConfigMap is read by a regex customManager that captures the tag only, so a digest pin cannot be written there. Same failure shape as above, on the renovate/k3s branch -- which means a k3s patch bump would have died with it. The ansible CronJobs carry the same image as volumes[].image.reference WITH a digest, read by a separate customManager, and keep their digest updates.
Untagged by design: the system-upgrade-controller derives the tag from the Plan's version at run time, and a digest on the base reference would break that concatenation.

Lives in the vendored upstream controller.yaml, which the kustomization keeps byte-for-byte so a re-vendor is an overwrite. Tag bumps there are tolerated; a digest would silently outlive the next re-vendor. Listed in .ci/image-pin-allowlist for the same reason.

Merging a k3s bump rolls all three control-plane nodes unattended. The bot's global config automerges every non-major update for '*', so this must opt out explicitly or a patch release would restart the control plane with nobody watching. rancher/kubectl rides along so the drain kubectl and the Plan version land in one PR when both have a patch pending -- they are independent release streams, so grouping cannot guarantee they always move together, and it is the minor gate below that keeps the skew in policy. The tag lives in three places: the controller's ConfigMap and the three ansible hypervisor-upgrade CronJobs, each read by its own customManager below.
Same for Flux: merging it rolls the controllers that do the deploying.

Minor upgrades of either are deliberate, one at a time, and gated on a runbook -- k3s because upstream permits no minor skipping and each minor has its own removals, Flux because each minor drops the APIs the last deprecated and carries its own Kubernetes floor. The EOL alerting is what should prompt them, not a PR. Patch updates stay in scope.

The drain kubectl must never run ahead of the k3s minor it drains for. k3s minors are gated above and move by runbook, so this one moves in that same PR -- if the bot could open a kubectl minor on its own it would break the skew policy in the one direction nothing else checks.

Renovate publishes its Docker image a few minutes before its npm package. validate-renovate.yaml checks the config against renovate@<image tag> on npm, so a bump opened inside that window fails CI with ETARGET until the bot rebases -- it did, twice, on 2026-09-12. Only version bumps move the tag the workflow reads, so digest and pin updates are left alone: they carry no usable timestamp and a blanket age would withhold them forever.

customManagers.description: The k3s version the system-upgrade-controller Plan rolls the nodes to. Nothing else tracks it: k3s is installed on the hosts by a shell script, so it is neither an image nor an apt package, and it drifted six months past EOL unnoticed before this existed.

The Flux version the operator distributes. Renovate has no manager for the fluxcd.controlplane.io FluxInstance CRD, and neither the flux nor kubernetes managerFilePatterns match a filename without 'helm' in it, so this was invisible too.

The kubectl that performs the node drain, pinned in a ConfigMap data field. The kubernetes manager only reads `image:` fields in pod specs, so this was invisible to it -- the two files that carry it both instruct a human to bump it alongside the Plan version, and the first bot-generated k3s PR could not have. The versioning regex is anchored to exclude the -amd64/-arm64 tags rancher/kubectl publishes beside each release.

The same kubectl, mounted into the ansible hypervisor-upgrade Jobs as an image volume. rancher/kubectl has no shell to copy the binary out with, so it is a `volumes[].image.reference` rather than an initContainer `image:`, and the kubernetes manager does not read that field either. Third site of the tag; the k3s packageRules above govern it like the other two.
